title: Dispatcher
explain: A dispatcher is a centralized matching and delivery layer between where tasks wait and the workers that run them. It takes over 'which queue next?' and 'which worker gets this?' so workers do not each carry that logic. Workers long-poll it with their free capacity, it hands out leased tasks under a global fairness policy, and it advances upstream offsets only when work is safely done.
model:
**Without it:** M priority queues, N workers, and each worker polls all queues with its own 80/20 dice. The real cost is not M x N connections (a Kafka consumer multiplexes topics) but that **scheduling policy and consumption state are copied into every worker**: no global fairness, quota or backpressure.

**With it:**

```
High queue --+
             +--> Dispatcher replicas --lease/retry--> Worker pool
Low queue  --+     ingress | delivery        <--AcquireTask(slots)-- (long-poll)
```

Five parts: **queue adapters** (Kafka/SQS to a Task carrying source offset), **admission buffer** (bounded; pause the partition but keep calling `poll()`), **scheduler** (strict priority, weighted or deficit round robin, aging, reserved capacity, tenant quota), **task leases** (`READY -> LEASED -> ACKED`), **ack coordinator**.

Protocol: worker pulls with free slots; reply carries stable `task_id` and per-delivery `lease_id`; worker heartbeats, then idempotent `Complete(task_id, lease_id)`; stale `lease_id` gets `STALE_LEASE` ([lease](#/sd/f/lease), [fencing](#/sd/f/fencing-token)).

Kafka offsets: commit only the **contiguous completed prefix** per partition. HA: replicas in one consumer group, shard ownership, durable lease state, idempotent delivery.

details.q: 500 workers each poll three priority queues with 80/20 dice. What is the strongest argument for a dispatcher?
details.a: It centralizes the scheduling policy and consumption state (fairness, quotas, backpressure, offsets) that is otherwise duplicated and uncoordinated across 500 workers. Saying it removes connections is weak, since Kafka consumers already multiplex.

details.q: Push or pull between dispatcher and worker?
details.a: Worker-initiated long-poll that states free capacity: workers with no free slot send nothing, so there is natural backpressure, and the dispatcher still decides what to send by priority, aging and tenant quota. Blind push floods slow workers. Start with HTTP/gRPC long-poll; use a bidirectional stream only for very high throughput.

details.q: Why both a task_id and a lease_id?
details.a: task_id names the logical task and stays across retries; lease_id names one delivery attempt and changes each time. If worker A pauses past its lease and the task moves to B, A's late Complete(T, L1) is refused as STALE_LEASE because the current lease is L2. A's side effects still need idempotency by task_id.

details.q: Partition 0 has offsets 100 to 105; 100, 101, 103, 104 are done, 102 and 105 running. What offset do you commit?
details.a: 102: the next offset to read is the first one not yet continuously completed. Committing 105 would lose 102 on a crash. Track a completion bitmap per partition and only advance the contiguous prefix (the commit frontier).

Before handoff can lose tasks if the dispatcher crashes between commit and delivery (at-most-once). After the worker's ack is at-least-once: nothing lost, duplicates possible, so make work idempotent by task_id. Durable handoff writes the task to the dispatcher's own store first, then commits upstream, moving retry responsibility into the dispatcher.

details.q: How does a dispatcher avoid starving the low-priority queue?
details.a: Random 80/20 only gives a long-run average, not a bound on any one task. Use weighted or deficit round robin, aging so waiting raises priority, reserved capacity for low classes and per-tenant quotas. See [weighted scheduling](#/sd/f/weighted-scheduling) and [prioritized scheduling](#/sd/f/prioritized-scheduling).

details.q: What happens on a consumer-group rebalance?
details.a: The old owner stops issuing leases, drains or revokes in-flight tasks, commits the contiguous prefix and releases the partition. The new owner resumes from the committed offset. Epoch fencing on lease and state updates stops the old owner from writing after it lost the partition.

Temporal's matching service is the closest: workers long-poll for tasks when they have capacity. Kubernetes' scheduler is a dispatcher for pods, with queue sort then filter and score. SQS/RabbitMQ/Celery push priority to the broker or worker side, which leaves worker-side polling and prefetch effects.

prompts.q: Explain what a dispatcher is and what problem it solves, in about a minute.
points: Centralized matching layer between task queues and workers
Without it every worker copies selection policy and consumption state
Few dispatchers read queues, workers long-poll one unified API
Global fairness, quota, backpressure in one place
Leases, heartbeats, idempotent completion for reliability

prompts.q: Walk through one task's path and what the lease and offsets do.
points: Worker sends AcquireTask with free slots
Scheduler atomically moves READY to LEASED
Returns task_id, lease_id, deadline; heartbeat while running
Complete(task_id, lease_id) idempotent, stale lease refused
ACKED persisted, then contiguous offset prefix committed

prompts.q: Explain how the dispatcher avoids starvation and how it stays available.
points: Weighted or deficit round robin, aging, reserved capacity, tenant quotas
Replicas in one consumer group with partition ownership
Idempotent delivery since exactly-once is not promised

prompts.q: Defend the choice of at-least-once for a dispatcher.
points: Cannot tell 'not executed' from 'executed but ack lost'
Commit after durable ack avoids loss
Duplicates handled by idempotent effects keyed by task_id
Exactly-once only with effect and offset in one transaction
